items.headline: Greenland parliament votes to ban seabed mining until at least 2029
items.title: Greenland to introduce ban on seabed mining
items.scifi_hook: The Arctic island puts a pause on deep‑sea mineral grabs amid geopolitical tension.
items.eli5: Greenland passed a law stopping mining on the ocean floor for several years.
items.why: It could curb future supply of critical minerals from the seabed.
items.rationale: potentially reduces demand for deep‑sea nodules
items.text: Greenland Parliament has unanimously passed a resolution to introduce a ban on seabed mineral extraction, RMF24 reported Friday . The news comes a day after US President Donald Trump announced “massive oil, gas and mineral exploration” was set to begin on Greenland. Trump described the Danish Arctic island, which is run by a semi-autonomous government, as “our new and beautiful Greenland” in a social media post that hailed what he said were US gains from a security deal signed in September. The resolution stipulates the memorandum on deep-sea mining is to remain in force until the end of 2029, RMF24 reported, with the possibility of extension for further two-year periods. The legislation is expected to be passed in the first half of 2027. Deep-sea mining faces surprise risk of rocks catching fire Greenland has been caught up in a confrontation with Trump who has been saying since 2019 the US should buy or take the strategically located and mineral-rich island for security reasons. On several occasions, he refused to rule out force. Greenland has one of the world’s most significant underexplored critical mineral endowments, positioning the territory at the center of critical minerals and defense supply chain strategies. The Tanbreez property in Greenland, with a 28.2 million tonne TREO resource, has been ranked as one of the world’s top rare earth projects. items.headline: Canada to tighten rules on foreign minority investments in critical minerals
items.title: Canada’s new foreign investment rules: What critical minerals miners need to know
items.scifi_hook: New filing rules force overseas backers to seek Canadian approval before funding mines.
items.eli5: Canada will require foreign investors to notify the government before buying small stakes in mineral projects.
items.why: It may slow capital flow to Canadian critical‑minerals projects.
items.rationale: could limit foreign funding for miners
items.text: Canadian critical minerals companies will need to consider how they raise foreign capital as Ottawa prepares to implement new Investment Canada Act rules that will require certain types of minority investments into a mandatory pre-closing filing regime. The changes could have particular consequences for miners and developers that rely on strategic investors to finance exploration, feasibility work, and project development, Toronto- based partner in Cassels’ Competition & Foreign Investment Group Chris Hersh told MINING.COM in an interview. The legislation underpinning the new regime was enacted in 2024, but key provisions requiring regulations are set to take effect in early 2027. Under the coming rules, certain investments by non-Canadians in businesses operating in prescribed sensitive sectors will require notification before the transaction can be completed — and will target investments that do not involve an acquisition of control of a Canadian business. Currently, acquisitions of control of Canadian businesses that fall below the applicable net-benefit review threshold generally require a notification that can be submitted up to 30 days after implementation, while minority investments that do not trigger a mandatory filing can be voluntarily notified to obtain greater certainty under national security review provisions of the law. items.headline: WarpWare raises $1.2 M pre‑seed to reuse flight‑software with AI tools
items.title: WarpWare Closes Pre-Seed to Bring Agentic Tools to Flight Software
items.scifi_hook: AI‑driven platform aims to stop spacecraft teams from rebuilding code for every mission.
items.eli5: WarpWare builds AI software that lets space engineers reuse code instead of starting from scratch each time.
items.why: It could cut development time and cost for future spacecraft.
items.text: For spacecraft software teams, every new program can feel like Groundhog Day. CO-based WarpWare closed its $1.2M pre-seed round today to expand what it calls an AI-enabled engineering platform for space missions. The round—raised through SAFEs—was primarily angel-funded. Angel groups including the Rockies Venture Club, Cowtown Angels, and the Aggie Angel Network joined individual angels and two space-focused early-stage funds, Vesper Alpha and Marlboro Lane Ventures. “Roughly 80% of the space software stack is expensive and time-consuming to build, but it is not proprietary,” WarpWare CEO and cofounder Alex Reynolds told Payload via email. Origin story: WarpWare grew out of a question the founders had while working at Sierra Space: How much of the company’s flight software could be reused for a new vehicle? The answer—according to Reynolds and COO Mickey Mathew , also a cofounder—was almost none. “Most teams are building many of the same foundational capabilities,” Reynolds said. Engineers often build flight software, guidance, navigation and control (GN&C), simulation and testing environments from scratch for each new program—dragging out timelines, raising costs, and adding technical risk, WarpWare officials say. WarpWare replaces that ground-up approach with one connected platform covering flight software, GN&C, simulation, and testing. items.headline: EraDrive secures $13M DoD award for autonomous satellite modules
items.title: Exclusive: EraDrive Lands $13M DoD Award For Autonomy Module
items.scifi_hook: A tiny startup’s AI brains will pilot military satellites, bypassing Earth‑bound bottlenecks.
items.eli5: EraDrive’s vision‑based module lets satellites make their own decisions without ground control.
items.why: Autonomous sats could speed up missions and reduce reliance on limited downlink capacity.
items.rationale: defense contractors may see increased demand
items.text: EraDrive, the Palo Alto, CA-based startup building autonomous capabilities for satellites, won a $13M DoD award, under which the Space Force will buy an undisclosed number of the company’s Era-Node vision-based autonomy modules. The Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies (APFIT) award is intended to provide direct procurement funding for new capabilities, unlike R&D-focused awards such as SBIR and STTR. EraDrive’s award creates an accelerated pathway for the Space Force to acquire Era-Nodes for future spacecraft. “Getting a small company’s technology onto a government contract usually takes years. Working with the APFIT office and NASA Ames, we got EraDrive selected and on contract within the same fiscal year. That’s the pace we need to keep up with what the commercial sector is building,” Lawrence Robertson, the Air Force’s lead for space experiments, told Payload via email. Keys to the castle: Autonomous capabilities for military sats have been on the DoD’s wish list for years. While serving as the Space Force’s top acquisition official in 2024, Frank Calvelli said autonomous sats would be vital to helping the DoD get around downlink bottlenecks.
